컵을 옆에서만 보면 속이 찼는지 비었는지 모른다. 위에서 자를 넣어 바닥: If you look at a cup only from the side, you can't tell whether it's full or empty. If you put a ruler in from the top and measure down to the bottom, you know that length is empty. But if you try to put the ruler in from the side, the cup wall blocks it, and you can't measure the inside.
<b>깊이 사진</b>은 픽셀마다 카메라에서 표면까지의 거리 d를 담는다: A depth map stores, for each pixel, the distance d from the camera to the surface. Among the voxels projected onto that pixel, the ones closer to the camera than d are empty (free-space carving[1]). We erase more of these from the visual hull carved from 8 silhouettes (2-4). Depth also measures only what is visible, so to carve the inside of the cup, you have to measure from an angle where the inside is visible.

목격자 한 명이 \"저기는 비어 있었다\"고 잘못 말하면 엉뚱한 결론이: If one witness wrongly says "that spot was empty," you reach a wrong conclusion. If you accept a claim only when two or more people say the same thing, one person's mistake has less effect.
깎은 머그컵을 깎을 때 쓰지 않은 <b>봉인된 새 각도</b> 6개에서: We draw the carved mug from 6 sealed new angles that were not used for carving, and count the pixels whose depth matches the true depth within 0.1. Real depth sensors have depth noise. If one noisy reading says "empty," it punches through the wall. Erasing only when two or more maps agree that it is "empty" (voting) makes the result less sensitive to noise.

One way is to check whether colors agree across many photos. Another is NeRF, which learns density and color at each point[4]. Part 3 goes the opposite direction: once we have 3D, "draw less and fill in with AI."
깊이 사진 k장 각각이 \"칸 p는 비었다\"를 eₖ(p) ∈ {0, 1: When each of k depth maps says "voxel p is empty" as e_k(p) ∈ {0, 1}, we erase p if Σₖ eₖ(p) ≥ v (v = 1 or 2). If, at noise σ, the probability that one map wrongly calls a wall voxel "empty" is q, then with v = 2 the probability of erasing it by mistake falls roughly on the order of q² (assuming the noise across photos is independent). Scoring is, for each sealed camera c, the fraction of pixels where |Ẑᶜ(pixel) − Zᶜ(pixel)| < 0.1. If the drawn side is empty, it counts as wrong.

블록을 종류별로 나누려고 자를 들었다. 보이는 가로·세로를 재면 같은 막: To sort blocks by kind, you pick up a ruler. Measuring the visible width and height, the same bar becomes a "wide block" when lying down and a "tall block" when standing. Measuring the long and short sides fixes orientation, but since each company's cell size differs, big T-shapes and small bars get confused. Also, T and L shapes are both 3×2 cells, so length alone cannot tell them apart. What separates them is the number of branches. A T-shape's middle cell splits in three directions.
k-평균은 특징 숫자들의 차이(거리)로 \"가깝다\"를 정한다. 그래서: k-means decides "closeness" by the differences (distance) between feature values. So features with a wide range of numbers decide the result. If you put the number of branches (2–3) next to the long side (18–60 mm) as is, the branch count gets buried. With standardization, where you subtract each feature's mean and divide by its standard deviation, every feature is on the same scale.

Instead of the size of the numbers, we look at "how far, relative to the typical spread," and the T-shapes neatly gathered.
Still fooled by size → create a feature that isn't fooled by size (100%). Even after standardizing, squares and L-shapes mixed as "small with small, big with big." As k grows, this value always decreases. So we pick the bend, not the smallest value (elbow method)[3]. We also look at the silhouette score, which shows how far groups are from each other[4]. 가족 족보를 아래에서부터 그린다. 가장 닮은 형제끼리 먼저 묶고, 그 형: Draw a family tree from the bottom up. First group the siblings who look most alike, then group those siblings with cousins, then with second cousins. After drawing it all, "how many branches to look at" is decided by where you cut the tree with scissors.
처음에는 그림 하나가 한 묶음이다. 가장 가까운 두 묶음을 합치기를 하나: At first each picture is its own group. Repeat merging the two closest groups until only one remains, and a tree (dendrogram) forms. Measuring "distance between groups" by the closest pair is single linkage, by the average is average linkage, and by the farthest pair is complete linkage[5][6]. This is hierarchical clustering.

PSNR: 픽셀 값이 0~1일 때 <span class=\"num\">P: PSNR: with pixel values from 0 to 1, PSNR = 10 · log₁₀(1 / MSE), where MSE is the mean squared error against the answer. If the root of the error is halved, MSE drops to a quarter and PSNR rises by 10 · log₁₀4 ≈ 6 dB.

<b>거꾸로 대신 앞으로 여러 번.</b> 사진에서 숫자를 바로 계산하지: Forward many times instead of backward. You can't compute the numbers from the photo directly, so you draw a photo from the numbers and compare.
<b>비교가 방향을 알려 준다.</b> 빨강이 오른쪽에 많으면 몽타주를: The comparison tells you the direction. If there's a lot of red on the right, move the sketch right; if there's red at the top or bottom, increase the height. People can tell the direction just by looking at the picture.
<b>숫자 넷이면 몇 번이면 된다.</b> 손으로 해 보면 20번 안팎에: Four numbers take only about 20 tries. Working by hand, about 20 tries can bring the misfit below 5%.

수식으로 보기 — 역렌더링을 최적화로\u0001: The math — inverse rendering as optimization
Let the numbers be θ = (radius, height, left-right, up-down), the renderer R, and the photo I. Inverse rendering becomes θ* = argmin_θ L(R(θ), I). Here L is the silhouette misfit 1 − |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B| (the overlap ratio, IoU, subtracted from 1). Using the renderer only in the forward direction, without solving it backward, is the core of "analysis by synthesis"[1].
빨강이 보이는 쪽으로 넓히고, 파랑이 보이는 쪽은 줄이고. 해 보니 생각: Widen toward where the red shows, and shrink where the blue shows. Turns out it's faster than you'd think!
격자와 무작위 — 같은 81장, 다른 결과\u0001: Grid vs. random — the same 81 drawings, different results
<span class=\"lvtag g\">모델: 격자 = 숫자마다 n칸: Model: grid = all combinations of n levels per number · random = 81 arbitrary drawsEveryday: searching for lost keys on a playground — walk in rows or scatter?
운동장에서 열쇠를 찾는다. 바둑판처럼 줄 맞춰 걸으면 빠짐없어 보이지만,: You're looking for your keys on the playground. Walking in neat rows looks thorough, but within a fixed number of steps, the gaps between rows get wide. Scattering and checking here and there looks at more places with the same number of steps.
<b>격자 찾기</b>는 숫자마다 범위를 칸으로 나눠 모든 조합을 그린다: Grid search divides each number's range into levels and draws every combination. With 81 drawings and 4 numbers, each number gets only 3 levels. Random search tries a different value for each number in all 81 drawings. When only a few numbers strongly affect the result, random samples those numbers more densely[2]. As the number of numbers grows, the grid's count grows by multiplication (curse of dimensionality).

4 numbers, 81 sketches: grid 17.7%, random 11.2%. The grid tried the radius at only three values: 0.73, 1.0, and 1.27.
<b>격자를 256장으로 늘려도 12.7%.</b> 숫자마다 4칸이면 4: Grid with 256 sketches is still 12.7%. With 4 levels per number, that's 4⁴ = 256 sketches. Still worse than 81 random sketches (11.2%). Each extra number multiplies the count.
<b>숫자 2개면 둘 다 괜찮다.</b> 81장을 숫자 2개에 쓰면 격자: With 2 numbers, both work fine. If you spend 81 sketches on 2 numbers, the grid has 9 levels per number: 4.4% (random 1.1%).

수식으로 보기 — 장 수와 숫자 수\u0001: The math — number of drawings and number of numbers
숫자 d개, 숫자마다 n칸인 격자는 <span class=\"num\">: A grid of d numbers with n levels each needs nᵈ drawings. With the same B drawings, a grid gives B^{1/d} levels per number (B = 81, d = 4 gives 3 levels). Random B drawings see B different values for each number. If only k numbers, fewer than d, decide the result, random samples those k numbers at about B levels each, while the grid sees only B^{1/d}[2].
같은 81장인데 격자는 같은 반지름을 27번씩 그렸어. 무작위는 한 번도: Same 81 drawings: the grid drew the same radius 27 times, while random never repeated a single one. That's how you spend money wisely.
다듬기와 모호함 — 촘촘히, 그러나 느리게\u0001: Refinement and ambiguity — dense, but slow
<span class=\"lvtag g\">모델: 숫자마다 ±보폭 시험: Model: try ±step for each number → keep it if it's better, otherwise halve the stepEveryday: nudge a radio dial to tune it
옛날 라디오는 다이얼을 조금씩 돌려 소리가 가장 깨끗한 곳을 찾는다. 지: Old radios: you turn the dial little by little to find the cleanest sound. If you overshoot, you go back and turn in smaller and smaller steps. With one dial it's quick; with dozens, it takes all day.
무작위 81장의 최선에서 출발해, 숫자마다 조금 키워 보고 줄여 보며 나: Starting from the best of the 81 random sketches, nudge each number up and down, and keep changes that improve things (refinement). If a full round brings no improvement, halve the step. With 4 numbers, one round is 8 sketches. And even when the misfit approaches 0, you must separately check whether the answer is unique (ambiguity, 2-1).

<b>0.6%까지.</b> 무작위 최선(11.2%)에서 몽타주 96장을: Down to 0.6%. From the random best (11.2%), we drew 96 more sketches to refine, and the misfit went to 0.6%. The radius found is 1.12, the height 1.72 (true values 1.12, 1.74).
<b>숫자가 많으면 느리다.</b> 한 바퀴마다 숫자 수 × 2장을 그린: More numbers is slower. Each round draws 2 sketches per number. Representing a real 3D shape with thousands of numbers means thousands of sketches per round.
<b>골짜기.</b> 카메라 거리를 모른다고 하면, 컵 크기와 거리를 함: The valley. If we don't know the camera distance, answers that change cup size and distance together form a diagonal band, and all of them match the photo well. Where refinement stops within the band depends on where it started.

렌더링 R은 3D 장면 θ(모양, 크기, 위치, 재질)를 사진 I로 보낸: Rendering R sends a 3D scene θ (shape, size, position, material) to a photo I: I = R(θ). Inverse rendering finds θ from I. If there are different θ₁ and θ₂ with R(θ₁) = R(θ₂) (a hidden handle, size and distance), the photo alone cannot tell them apart. Such problems are called "ill-posed inverse problems," and they are solved with more photos or assumptions (prior knowledge).

<b>기울기</b>는 숫자를 아주 조금 바꿨을 때 어긋남이 얼마나 바뀌는: Gradient is how much the mismatch changes when you change a parameter very slightly (derivative). But the silhouette's pixels are 0 or 1. If you increase the radius by 0.001 and the edge doesn't cross into the next pixel, no pixel changes and the mismatch stays the same. So the mismatch is a staircase, with gradient 0 on the treads and endlessly large at the edges[2].

The brackets are 1 if true, 0 if false. ∂Sᵢ/∂θ = 0 (except at the instant mᵢ = 0). So the gradient of L = 1 − IoU is also almost always zero. If you measure with the difference (L(θ+δ) − L(θ−δ))/2δ, you get 0 by bad luck, and if you happen to catch the edge, it swings wildly depending on δ (code 1, ③).

흐린 안경을 쓰면 컵의 가장자리가 뚝 끊기지 않고 서서히 옅어진다. 컵을: When you wear blurry glasses, the edge of a cup doesn't break off sharply but fades gradually. Even if the cup gets a little bigger, the faint band at the edge gets a bit darker. Even tiny changes show up.
광선이 컵에 가장 가까이 간 거리 m을 재고, 픽셀이 덮인 정도를 0~1: Measure the closest distance m the ray gets to the cup, and draw the degree of pixel coverage as a value between 0 and 1 (soft silhouette). Rays that pass through the cup are near 1 (the thinner the wall, the less dark when τ is large), far outside is 0, and near the edge it's in between. The larger the blur width τ, the wider the blur. Now even a small change in the parameters changes the edge pixel values slightly, so the mismatch becomes a smooth slide, with a gradient everywhere[3]. The gradient is obtained by backward calculation rather than by drawing again.

수식으로 보기 — 부드러운 실루엣과 거꾸로 계산\u0001: The math — soft silhouette and backward calculation
<span class=\"num\">Sᵢ = σ(−mᵢ/τ) = 1/(1: Sᵢ = σ(−mᵢ/τ) = 1/(1 + emᵢ/τ), L = (1/N) Σ (Sᵢ − Tᵢ)² (T is the photo). By the chain rule, ∂L/∂θ = (1/N) Σ 2(Sᵢ − Tᵢ) · (−Sᵢ(1 − Sᵢ)/τ) · ∂mᵢ/∂θ. Since mᵢ is the value of the distance function at the closest point p* on the ray, ∂mᵢ/∂θ = ∂f(p*; θ)/∂θ. You only need to re-measure the distance function at p*, so there's no need to draw again. Soft Rasterizer uses the same idea for the triangles of a mesh (turning the distance to the boundary into a probability)[3].

<b>주성분 분석</b>은 240장이 가장 크게 다른(출렁이는) 방향을: Principal component analysis finds the direction in which the 240 images differ most (swing most). That direction is a principal component, and when shown as a picture, it is an eigenface. Subtract the mean face from a face, multiply by the eigenfaces pixel by pixel, and add up to get one number. Using eigenfaces 1 and 2 to make two numbers gives a point on the map (latent space). Since every pixel gets mixed in a little, the point doesn't shift much even when the drawing shifts slightly. The usefulness of the map is measured by nearest-neighbor matching.

So if you walk in a straight line between two points on the map and unfold, you get exactly the same as overlapping the two faces semi-transparently. Unfolding from the middle of the map (where no face exists) gives the mean face, a ghost where all the characters overlap. A curved map, or one that plausibly fills in empty areas, needs a nonlinear method[4].

Computation is fast (one eigenvalue problem), the same data always gives the same answer, and the axes (eigenfaces) can be explained by looking at pictures. That is why it's still the first tool people use when they first look at data.

A straight line on the map becomes a straight line in picture space (overlapping). Nonlinear maps (t-SNE[4], autoencoders) lack this property, so they can follow curved paths. 원래 해상도에 비해 가로·세로를 몇 %로 그리는지. 그리는 픽셀은 그 제: The percentage of native width and height that is drawn. The number of pixels drawn drops by the square of this ratio.
작은 그림을 큰 그림으로 키우는 일. 비어 있는 픽셀을 무엇으로 채울지가: Enlarging a small picture into a large one. The question is what to fill the empty pixels with.
가장 가까운 작은 픽셀의 색을 그대로 복사한다. 계단이 진다.\u0001: Copies the color of the closest small pixel as it is. Leaves jagged edges.
가까운 작은 픽셀 넷을 거리만큼 섞는다. 계단 대신 흐려진다.\u0001: Blends the four nearest small pixels by their distances. Blurs instead of leaving jagged edges.
작은 그림에 없던 세부를 배워서 그럴듯하게 채우며 키우는 일.\u0001: Enlarging a picture while learning and filling in detail that wasn't in the small picture.
픽셀 하나에 여러 점의 색을 찍어 평균하는 비싼 그리기. 경계가 부드럽다: An expensive way of drawing in which the colors of several points are sampled and averaged for each pixel. Edges come out smooth.
정답 그림과 얼마나 가까운지를 dB로 잰 점수. 클수록 가깝고, 오차가: A score in dB measuring how close a picture is to the answer. Higher means closer. Halving the error adds about 6 dB.

\"학습 화면 12장, 정답은 16점으로 비싸게. 데이터에 투자한 만큼: "12 training screens, with answers drawn expensively at 16 points. You get back what you invest in data."
3-1에서 배운 업스케일러는 한 장 안에서 그럴듯하게 짐작했다. 그런데: The upscaler from 3-1 made plausible guesses within a single frame. But game screens flow by at dozens of frames per second. If you shift the sampling spot slightly from scene to scene (jitter), then when you collect many frames, each pixel accumulates real colors from several spots. The problem is motion. When blocks fall, memories stay in the wrong place and trail behind. Track them with motion vectors, and cut away memories that don't match. These are the second and third ingredients DLSS 2.0 receives.
<b>배운 필터</b>는 ②의 길잡이 필터를 반경 1·2·3·5·7·9로: The learned filter runs the guided filter from ② at radii 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, and 9, then a small neural network decides how much of each result to blend in at every pixel. Its inputs are seven things: the ray count, the distance to the edge, the shimmer at that spot, the difference between the wide and narrow filter results, and brightness. It learned in advance from eight training scenes drawn with 1, 2, 4, and 8 rays, adjusting itself to get close to the correct image (128 rays). Letting a network choose the filter shape (the blend weights) for each pixel comes from the learned denoisers used in film rendering[3].

NVIDIA는 DLSS 3.5의 레이 리컨스트럭션이 손으로 조정한 디노이: NVIDIA says the Ray Reconstruction in DLSS 3.5 replaced hand-tuned denoisers with a single AI neural network, so the car headlight light in Cyberpunk 2077 that used to smear now comes out sharp<sup>[1]</sup>. The network on this page is a toy with 12 hidden units, but the idea is the same. Instead of a person writing the blending rules, the network learns them from correct images.

재료 <span class=\"num\">x(p) = [log₂(광선 수: Inputs x(p) = [log₂(ray count)/3, distance to edge/6, shimmer, |Ê₉ − Ê₂|·3, |Ê₅ − Ê₂|·3, Ê₃, 1]. Hidden units h = max(0, W₁x + b₁) (12 units), weights w = softmax(W₂h + b₂) (7 values: unfiltered light and radii 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9). Result Ê(p) = Σ_k w_k(p) Ê_k(p). Training: over every pixel of 8 training scenes × 4 ray counts, we used Adam for 8,000 steps to reduce (Ê − answer)². The two test scenes were not used for training. Having the network output the filter weights directly is a tiny version of KPCN (kernel-predicting network)[3].

Our everyday analogy is Everyday D (an ID photo at a photo studio, an exam envelope). The bust is a 3D model built from a few balls (a head, two buns, a body), which this page draws directly with rays. Two people who look like the assistant (pink bob, brown bun) were made the same way. The light is a long bar light above and in front of the assistant, and the camera circles the assistant.
NVIDIA는 DLSS 4에서 업스케일(작게 그리기), 다중 프레임 생성: NVIDIA says DLSS 4 uses upscaling (drawing small), multi-frame generation (in-between frames), and Ray Reconstruction (filtering rays) together, so that “AI creates 15 of every 16 pixels”<sup>[1]</sup>. Let's line up the ingredients we learned one at a time.

한 장의 일 <span class=\"num\">= ρ · N_px ·: Work per frame = ρ · N_px · (1 + N_shadow) + N_geo. N_px is the number of pixels drawn (96² or 48²), N_shadow is shadow rays per pixel (16 or 1), ρ is the fraction of frames truly drawn (1 or ½), and N_geo is the geometry rays for motion info (96² when accumulation or in-between frames are on). Baseline = 96² × 17. Quality is the average PSNR over scenes 8–15. The correct image was drawn with 3×3 points per pixel and 16 shadow rays, spread evenly. Time accumulation uses memory only when the same object point was visible in an earlier scene (3D distance within 0.08).

Compare pixels with the training photos (front −75° to 75°, every 15°, two photos each for three people), and output the name of the most similar one. 친구를 앞모습으로만 알았다면 뒷모습으로는 못 알아볼 수 있다. 사진관에서: If you only knew a friend from the front, you might not recognize them from behind. You could have them walk around at a photo studio, take photos, and learn from those. But keep the real test paper in an envelope and open it only during the exam. If you peek early, you get a score but don't learn your real ability.
앞쪽 사진으로만 배우면 뒤에서 찍은 시험 사진을 거의 못 알아본다. 그런: If you learn only from front photos, you'll barely recognize test photos taken from behind. But we have a 3D model and a renderer. By shooting training photos every 15° around the full loop, the renderer knows the angles and labels (synthetic data), just as the renderer made the correct images in 3-1. Scoring uses only the 120 sealed test data photos (any angle, 40 photos each for the three people). If test photos mix into training, that's data leakage[3].

Kinect's body-pose recognition was trained on countless 3D people made from motion-capture recordings, using rendered depth images<sup>[2]</sup>. But if the gap between real and rendered photos is large, what was learned doesn't transfer well. This page drew the test photos with the same renderer, so it's an easy case with no such gap.

3-1의 배운 업스케일러는 ×3에서 다시 힘이 빠졌다. 한 장에 찍히지: The upscaler you learned in 3-1 lost strength again at ×3. A thin line that was not captured in a single frame cannot be restored exactly by any AI.
게임은 어차피 1초에 수십 장을 그린다. 장면마다 조금씩 다른 자리를 찍: The game draws dozens of frames per second anyway. If you record a slightly different spot in each frame, then when you gather them it is as if you split an expensive supersampling across many frames.
NVIDIA는 DLSS 2.0이 작게 그린 그림과 함께 모션 벡터, 앞: NVIDIA explains that DLSS 2.0 takes as input the low-resolution image together with motion vectors and the result of earlier frames<sup>[1][2]</sup>. This is a big change from 1.0, which learned separately for each game<sup>[3]</sup>.
큰 그림 — 찍고, 따라가고, 버리고, 섞는다\u0001: The big picture — shoot, follow, discard, mix
장면마다 지터 자리로 작게 그린다. 앞 장면의 기억을 모션 벡터만큼 끌어: Each frame is drawn small at a jitter spot. Pull the memory of the earlier frame by the motion vector, cut away memory that does not match the current frame, then mix in the new points to become the memory for the next frame
매번 다른 자리 한 점\u0001: One point at a different spot each time
③ 안 맞으면 자르기\u0001: ③ Cut if it doesn't match
지금 이웃 색 범위로\u0001: By the current neighboring color range
= 지금 장면의 큰 화면\u0001: = the large image of the current frame
지금 장면의 작은 그림은 ③ 자르기의 기준도 된다\u0001: The small image of the current frame is also the reference for cutting in ③
지터 — 장면마다 점을 조금씩 옮겨 찍기\u0001: Jitter — shift the sample points slightly from frame to frame
<span class=\"lvtag g\">모델: 픽셀 안의 찍는 자리를: Model: move the sampling position inside a pixel along a Halton sequence, and gather those points into the large pixelEveryday: take several photos in the dark and stack them
창살 너머 풍경을 보려고 고개를 조금씩 움직이며 여러 번 본다. 한 번에: To see the scenery behind bars, you move your head slightly and look several times. At any one moment part of the view is blocked by the bars, but if you combine what you saw from different positions, the whole scene forms in your mind. Looking a hundred times from the same spot still leaves the blocked part blocked.
작은 그림의 픽셀은 한 점의 색만 가져간다. 장면마다 그 점을 픽셀 안의: A small image's pixel takes only one color. Each frame moves that sample to a different spot inside the pixel (jitter). The spots do not overlap; they are chosen with the Halton sequence, which fills empty spots evenly[6]. If you mix colors into the large pixel where that point falls and gather them (temporal accumulation), it is as if an expensive supersampling were split across many frames[4].

큰 픽셀 p의 기억 Hₜ(p)에 이번 장면의 점 색 c가 떨어지면 <sp: The memory Hₜ(p) of large pixel p receives the current frame's point color c, Hₜ(p) = (1 − α)·Hₜ₋₁(p) + α·c, α = max(1 / (n + 1), α_min). n is the number of points gathered at that pixel. At first it gathers like an average (1/(n+1)); later it keeps reflecting new frames little by little at α_min (0.1 here).
할턴 수열: 정수 i를 b진법으로 쓰고 소수점 반대편으로 뒤집은 수. b: Halton sequence: write integer i in base b and flip it across the decimal point. With b = 2 and 3 on the horizontal and vertical axes, it fills empty spots evenly: (0.5, 0.33), (0.25, 0.67), (0.75, 0.11), …

게임은 블록을 직접 움직이니, 픽셀마다 앞 장면에서 얼마나 움직였는지(<: Since the game moves the blocks itself, it can tell for each pixel how far it moved since the earlier frame (motion vector). When fetching the current pixel's memory, you pull it from the spot traced back by that distance. Gathering without motion vectors leaves the old color behind, dragging a tail: ghosting. DLSS 1.0 struggled with moving scenes, and 2.0 improved greatly by receiving motion vectors[3].

Where the block moved aside, the newly revealed background has no memory to follow, yet the old block color remains; and each fetch blurs it a little with bilinear blending. The average is 22.0 dB, close to using a single frame.

큰 픽셀 (x, y)의 움직임이 장면 하나에 (0, v)이면 <span: If the motion of large pixel (x, y) in one frame is (0, v), then H′ₜ(x, y) = Hₜ₋₁(x, y − v). Since v is not an integer multiple of the pixel size, the four surrounding pixels are blended bilinearly to fetch it. When this blending repeats every frame, the memory gradually blurs. Real games use sharper interpolation such as bicubic[5].
봐, 꼬리 생겼지. 모션 벡터로 따라가도 블록이 비켜난 자리는 틀린 기억: See, a tail appeared. Even when you follow with motion vectors, the spots the blocks moved away from hold wrong memory. You have to throw out what's wrong.
믿을 수 없는 기억 잘라내기 — 지금 장면의 이웃 색이 기준\u0001: Cutting untrustworthy memory — the current frame's neighboring colors are the reference
<span class=\"lvtag g\">모델: 기억 색을 지금 장면: Model: clip the memory color to the min–max of the 3×3 neighboring colors of the current frame (clamping)Everyday: when memory and what's in front of you are too different, trust what's in front of you
어제 본 책상 위에 빨간 컵이 있었다고 기억한다. 오늘 책상 주변 어디에: You remember a red cup on the desk yesterday. If there is no red anywhere around the desk today, the cup must have been removed. You discard the memory and trust what you see now. But if you are too strict, you also erase real objects that are hard to see because the light is dim today, marking them as "gone."
끌어온 기억 색이 지금 장면 작은 그림의 3×3 이웃 색 범위 밖이면,: If the fetched memory color is outside the 3×3 neighboring color range of the current frame's small image, clip it to the edge of that range (clamping). If it was clipped a lot, the memory at that spot starts over. This is a rule widely used in game temporal anti-aliasing (TAA)[4][5]. Ghosting decreases, but the real detail you gathered with difficulty through jitter can be clipped too.

<b>손으로 만든 규칙의 한계.</b> 한 가지 규칙으로는 두 경우를 다: The limits of a hand-made rule. One rule can hardly handle both cases well. Real games are harder still, with translucent smoke, reflections, and on-screen text, where motion vectors are often wrong.
DLSS 2.0은 작게 그린 그림, 모션 벡터, 앞 장면의 결과를 함께: DLSS 2.0 receives the small image, the motion vectors, and the result of earlier frames together. Instead of hand-made rules for how to gather and what to discard, a neural network learns them<sup>[1][2]</sup>. The ground truth is the expensively rendered image, as in 3-1.

큰 픽셀 p가 속한 작은 픽셀의 3×3 이웃 색을 c₁…c₉라 하면, 색: If the 3×3 neighboring colors of the small image containing large pixel p are c₁…c₉, then for each color component H″(p) = min(max(H′(p), min cᵢ), max cᵢ). If the amount clipped is large (here, more than 0.08), the gathered point count n of that pixel is reduced to 1 so the new point is reflected strongly.

The visual hull shows exactly the ceiling of "this is as far as silhouettes can take us." Concave places like the inside of the cup do not show up in silhouettes, no matter how many you gather<sup>[1]</sup>.

Pushing this idea into a neural network gives NeRF<sup>[3]</sup>. For each point in space, it learns "how filled it is and what color it is" to match many photos.

What one photo keeps is Kᶜ = {p : Sᶜ(πᶜ(p)) = 1}, the cone (column) formed by the rays from the camera through the silhouette. With many photos, H = ∩ᶜ Kᶜ. The true object X is always X ⊆ H[1].

여러 장으로 깎기 — 장 수보다 고르게\u0001: Carving from many photos: evenly spread matters more than the count
<span class=\"lvtag g\">모델: 시각 껍질 = 모든 실: Model: visual hull = overlap of all silhouette columnsEveryday: a sculptor turning a stone block while carving
A sculptor carves a stone block from the front, then turns it and carves from the side, then turns it again and carves more. If you carve only from the same direction, only the front gets shaped, and the side stays square.
사진마다 실루엣 기둥이 하나씩 생기고, 남는 덩어리는 기둥들이 <b>모두: Each photo creates one silhouette column, and the remaining mass is where all the columns overlap. This is called the visual hull[1]. The real cup is always inside it. The more evenly you take photos around the cup, the closer the hull gets to the cup. But there is a ceiling that no amount of photos can get past.

수식으로 보기 — 시각 껍질과 천장\u0001: The math: visual hull and ceiling
무한히 많은 방향에서 본 실루엣으로 얻는 껍질을 Laurentini는 시: Laurentini defined the visual hull VH(X) as the shape obtained from silhouettes seen from infinitely many directions[1]. Objects with the same silhouettes cannot be told apart, so the best silhouettes can give is VH(X). With n photos around the ring (at height 15°), X ⊆ VH(X) ⊆ Hₙ, and as n grows, Hₙ shrinks toward VH(X). For the mug, VH is the "cup with its inside filled in (+ handle)," so IoU(X, VH) = 2,504 / 7,840 ≈ 31.9% is the ceiling.
8장에서 16장으로 두 배를 썼는데 0.4%포인트? 이건 투자 대비 수익: Doubling from 8 to 16 photos only gave 0.4 percentage points? That is a terrible return on investment…
뚫린 구멍과 오목한 구멍 — 천장의 정체\u0001: Through hole and concave hole: the identity of the ceiling
<span class=\"lvtag g\">모델: 실루엣에 드러나는 구멍: Model: only holes that show up in silhouettes get carvedEveryday: a donut's hole shows, but the inside of a bowl does not show in the shadow
도넛을 세워 손전등을 비추면 그림자 가운데 구멍이 뚫려 보인다. 그릇은: Stand a donut up and shine a flashlight on it, and the shadow shows a hole in the middle. A bowl casts a shadow that is solid no matter which way you shine the light. You cannot tell from the shadow that the bowl is hollow.
손잡이 구멍은 <b>뚫린 구멍</b>이다. 맞는 방향(앞)에서 보면 빛이: The handle hole is a through hole. Seen from the right direction (the front), light passes through, so the silhouette has a hole too, and it is carved. The inside of the cup is a concave hole. Any ray through the inside of the cup first hits the wall or the rim, so the silhouette always looks like a "solid cup." That is why there is no basis for erasing the cells inside the cup[1]. To carve the inside of the cup, we need information other than silhouettes (color, depth)[2][3].

수식으로 보기 — 공간 깎기와 NeRF\u0001: The math: space carving and NeRF
공간 깎기<sup>[2]</sup>는 칸이 실루엣 안에 있는지 대신, 그: Space carving[2] asks, instead of whether a cell is inside the silhouette, whether the photos that see that cell show the same color (photo consistency). If they do not match, the cell is erased. This way, the bottom inside the cup, whose color differs from the rim as seen from above, can also be carved out, even in concave places. NeRF[3] does not erase cells as 0/1. Instead, it uses a neural network to hold a density σ and a color c at each point, and learns by gradients so that the color blended from points along a ray, Σ Tᵢ (1 − e−σᵢδᵢ) cᵢ, matches every photo (the sliding of 2-3). Silhouette carving is the simplest case: "no color, only 0/1."
그림자는 겉모양만 말해 줘. 속을 알고 싶으면 그림자 말고 다른 걸 물어: A shadow only tells you the outer shape. If you want to know what is inside, you have to ask something other than the shadow.
대결 — 8장 vs 64장, 머그컵 깎기\u0001: Duel: 8 photos vs 64 photos, carving the mug
초파리는 컵 둘레에 고르게 8장(높이 15°), 주판봇은 둘레를 돌며 높: The fruit fly takes 8 photos evenly around the cup (height 15°). AbaBot walks around the cup, changing the height as well, and takes 64 photos (alternating heights of 0°, 30°, 60°, and 85°). The side whose carved mass has the larger overlap with the real mug wins. If the difference is within 2 percentage points, it is a draw.

<b>광학 흐름</b>은 엔진 정보 없이 두 그림만 비교해, 픽셀마다 \: Optical flow compares only the two pictures, with no engine data, and finds for each pixel “where it moved”[4]. Screen effects like flames, shadows, and reflections are followed too, as long as they're visible. But it's a guess, so it can go wrong in flat areas or at edges. NVIDIA explains that DLSS 3 takes both optical flow and motion vectors because motion vectors can follow the road but not the shadow on it[1].

사이 자리 p의 움직임 <span class=\"num\">d* = ar: Motion at in-between spot p: d* = argmin_d Σ_{q∈window(p)} |A(q − d/2) − B(q + d/2)| + λ‖d‖². The window is 5×5, and d searches ±8 pixels horizontally and vertically in steps of 2 pixels. λ‖d‖² is a small penalty that keeps it from picking large motions on flat areas. Classic optical flow sets up formulas like this on the assumption that brightness carries over unchanged[4].

사이 장면을 만들려면 뒤 장면까지 다 그려야 한다. 그래서 뒤 장면은 사: To make an in-between frame, you have to draw the frame after it too. So the next real frame shows up later by as long as the in-between frames take to display first (latency). Hand input only lands on really rendered frames, so even at 4× the screen frames, the frames that respond to your hand stay the same. NVIDIA pairs frame generation with Reflex, which reduces the CPU and GPU waiting queues[1][2].

The display waits for the next real frame and shows the in-betweens first, so in this model it adds +16.7 ms at 2× and +25 ms at 4× (based on 30 real frames/sec). The more real frames there are (60 frames/sec), the smaller the added amount. Conversely, with few real frames, turning it on makes the delay feel bigger.

진짜 장면 간격 T(30장/초면 33.3 ms), 배수 k. 화면 장 수: Real-frame interval T (33.3 ms at 30 frames/sec), multiplier k. Frames on screen = k / T. To insert k − 1 in-between frames evenly between the previous and next real frames, the next real frame must be shown later by (k − 1)/k · T. The interval at which input lands is still T. 창문이 얼마나 보이는지 알고 싶어 눈을 감고 아무 데나 손가락으로 한 번: To find out how much of a window you can see, close your eyes and point your finger at random. A window means “bright,” a wall means “dark.” Point once and luck decides the answer. Point ten or a hundred times and average, and you approach “about 40% of the window is visible.” A photo taken in the dark is grainy for the same reason: each pixel gets few light particles, so luck plays a big role.
픽셀마다 천장 등의 아무 점으로 <b>광선</b>을 쏜다. 블록에 막히지: For each pixel, shoot a ray toward a random point on the ceiling light. The fraction not blocked by a block is the light that pixel receives. With few rays per pixel (rays per pixel, spp), neighboring pixels get different luck, which creates noise. The worst noise is at the edge of a shadow where only part of the light is blocked, the penumbra. Multiply the rays by N and the noise drops by √N, so you need 4× the rays to halve it.

A well-made app recognizes the boundary between face and background and doesn’t mix across it. How hard to push depends on the photo: dark photos get more, bright photos less.
<b>상자 필터</b>는 반경 안의 이웃 빛을 모두 똑같이 평균한다. 블: A box filter averages all the neighboring light within a radius equally, so light from blocks and background bleeds together. A guide filter looks at a noise-free guide image (which block is which), mixes only within the same block, and mixes more the closer the pixels are. It also filters only the light. The block's color (base color) has no noise, so it is removed first and multiplied back in after filtering. Real-time hand filters use these two standard tricks (filter only the light, protect edges with a guide)[2].
